301 redirects protect your Google rankings when you move or rename pages.
Forcing HTTPS everywhere avoids insecure mixed-content warnings for visitors.

faqs.a: Use 301 for permanent moves: renamed pages, merged content, HTTP to HTTPS, or a changed domain. Search engines transfer ranking signals to the new URL. Use 302 only when the move is genuinely temporary, like a short maintenance page or an A/B test, because Google keeps ranking the old URL.

Upload it to the root folder of your website (usually public_html or www) on an Apache server. The file name must be exactly .htaccess, starting with a dot. Most hosting file managers and FTP clients can show hidden dotfiles; enable that option if you cannot see it.
faqs.q: Where do I upload the .htaccess file?

faqs.a: A single typo in .htaccess can break the whole site with a 500 Internal Server Error, because Apache reads the file on every request. Download a backup of your current file first, change one thing at a time, and test in a private browser window after each upload.
faqs.q: Why did my site show a 500 error after editing .htaccess?

faqs.a: Redirect is simpler and handled by mod_alias. It matches the start of the URL path exactly. RewriteRule is more powerful and handled by mod_rewrite: it supports patterns, conditions, and query strings. For plain page-to-page moves, Redirect is enough; for HTTPS and www rules, RewriteRule is the standard choice.
faqs.q: What is the difference between Redirect and RewriteRule?

faqs.a: Keep important 301 redirects for at least one year. Google needs months to fully transfer signals, and old links from other sites keep sending visitors. For redirects tied to a rebrand or domain change, many site owners keep them permanently.
faqs.q: How long should I keep a 301 redirect?

faqs.a: Nginx does not read .htaccess at all. Equivalent redirects go in the server block of your Nginx configuration, for example: return 301 https://example.com$request_uri;. If your host uses Nginx, ask their support where to add redirect rules.
faqs.q: Does this work on Nginx hosting?

howTo: Add one rule per moved page: the old path (for example /old-page) and the full new URL.
Pick 301 for permanent moves or 302 for temporary ones.
Optionally tick Force HTTPS and choose a www rule.
Copy the output or download it as a .htaccess file.
Back up your current .htaccess, upload the new one to your site root, and test each redirect in a private window.
keyFacts: A .htaccess file is a configuration file for Apache web servers. It controls redirects, access rules, and URL rewriting per folder.
A 301 redirect means moved permanently. Browsers cache it and Google passes ranking signals to the new URL.
A 302 redirect means moved temporarily. Browsers re-check the old URL on every visit and Google keeps ranking it.
The Redirect directive matches the start of a path, so Redirect 301 /blog also catches /blog/post-1 automatically.
Forcing HTTPS with a RewriteRule protects login forms and payment pages from eavesdropping.

htaccess-redirect-generator.quickAnswer: A 301 redirect means a page moved permanently; a 302 means temporarily. In .htaccess the syntax is: Redirect 301 /old-page https://example.com/new-page. This tool builds those lines from a simple form, plus optional force-HTTPS and www rules, so you can copy or download a correct .htaccess file without learning Apache syntax.
htaccess-redirect-generator.tagline: Build correct 301 and 302 redirect rules for Apache with a simple form. No syntax to memorise.
htaccess-redirect-generator.workedExample:
You renamed /summer-sale to https://example.com/sale and want HTTPS everywhere:
1. Old path: /summer-sale. New URL: https://example.com/sale. Type: 301.
2. Tick Force HTTPS.
3. The tool generates:
   RewriteEngine On
   RewriteCond %{HTTPS} off
   RewriteRule ^(.*)$ https://%{HTTP_HOST}%{REQUEST_URI} [L,R=301]
   Redirect 301 /summer-sale https://example.com/sale
4. Upload to your site root and test both URLs. The old page now redirects permanently.
mistakes: Uploading without backing up the old file — one typo gives you a 500 error and a dead site. Keep a copy of the working .htaccess first.
Using 302 for a permanent move — 302 tells Google the move is temporary, so the old page keeps the ranking. Permanent moves need 301.
Never testing after upload — chains and loops are silent killers. Open every old URL yourself and confirm it lands in the right place.
Using it on Nginx hosting — .htaccess is an Apache file. On Nginx it's completely ignored and nothing will redirect.
Dropping the leading slash in old paths — /old-page and old-page are different to Apache. Without the slash, the rule never matches.
